**Urgent surgical repair** (never observe or merely suture conjunctiva): fresh **donor corneal/scleral/pericardial patch graft** + tension-free **vascularized conjunctival flap** (or buccal mucosal graft); **explant GDD** if recurrent exposure or infection occurs [2][3].
Mechanical tube-endothelium touch, aqueous jet turbulence, or shallow AC; accelerates endothelial loss (~10–15%/yr in AC tubes) [2][3].
Shorten or reposition tube into **ciliary sulcus** (pseudophakes) or **pars plana** (with complete PPV); perform **DMEK/DSAEK** after posterior tube relocation [2][3].
Iris incarceration, fibrin/blood clot, inflammatory membrane, or vitreous wick occluding internal ostium [2].
Fibrin/clot: **intracameral tPA (10–25 µg)**; iris/membrane: **argon iridoplasty / Nd:YAG laser**; vitreous: **Nd:YAG vitreolysis or anterior/pars plana vitrectomy** [1][2].
Thick fibrous Tenon's capsule around plate (classic 3–6 weeks post-Ahmed FP7 implantation) [2][3].
Early **aqueous suppressants** (to lower inflammatory cytokine flow into bleb), potent topical steroids, 5-FU/MMC needling, or surgical excision of anterior bleb capsule [2][3].
Fibrous bleb mass effect on superior oblique tendon (**pseudo-Brown syndrome** with superonasal placement) or rectus muscle entrapment [2][3].
Fresnel/ground-in **prisms**, capsule decompression/excision, targeted strabismus surgery, or relocating/exchanging to a lower-profile plate [2][3].
Excessive CW-TSCPC causing **fibrinous uveitis, CME, neurotrophic keratitis** (3 & 9 o'clock nerve injury), **phthisis bulbi**, or rarely **sympathetic ophthalmia** [1][2].

Intensive topical/periocular steroids + cycloplegics + NSAIDs; preserve 3 & 9 o'clock meridians; manage sympathetic ophthalmia urgently with **high-dose systemic corticosteroids + steroid-sparing immunosuppression** (mycophenolate/adalimumab) [1][2].

1.chapter: Complications of Incisional Glaucoma Surgery, Drainage Implants & Cyclodestruction
1.quote: Postoperative shallow anterior chambers are triaged by IOP and bleb height (pupillary block, aqueous misdirection, suprachoroidal hemorrhage vs. overfiltration, bleb leak, serous choroidal effusion). Tube exposure requires urgent patch grafting and vascularized conjunctival coverage.

2.book: Shields' Textbook of Glaucoma (7th Edition) — Allingham et al.
2.chapter: Management of Complications of Filtering Surgery & Glaucoma Drainage Devices
2.quote: Intraoperative suprachoroidal hemorrhage mandates immediate watertight wound closure and AC tamponade without premature drainage; delayed SCH is drained after 7–14 days of clot liquefaction if kissing, painful, or causing flat AC. Kissing serous choroidals and late ischemic MMC bleb leaks require surgical drainage and bleb excision with conjunctival advancement, respectively.

3.book: Gedde SJ et al. (TVT 5-Year Complications, Am J Ophthalmol 2012) & Budenz DL et al. (ABC 5-Year Complications, Ophthalmology 2015)
3.chapter: Long-Term Surgical Complications of Tube Shunts vs. Trabeculectomy
3.quote: Late tube-shunt complications include persistent corneal edema/endothelial failure, tube/plate erosion (~2–8%), diplopia/motility restriction, and hypertensive bleb encapsulation, whereas trabeculectomy carries higher rates of early wound/bleb leaks, hypotony maculopathy, and late bleb-related infection.

4.book: Busbee BG et al. (Ophthalmology 2004) & Leng T et al.
4.chapter: Microbiology, Clinical Presentation & Management of Bleb-Related Endophthalmitis (BRE)
4.quote: Late-onset bleb-related endophthalmitis is predominantly caused by virulent Streptococcus species, Haemophilus influenzae, and Staphylococcus aureus, strongly associated with inferior or leaking avascular blebs. Early pars plana vitrectomy with intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime is favored over tap-and-inject alone even at visual acuities better than light perception.

5.book: Shahid H & Salmon JF (Br J Ophthalmol 2012); Dave P et al.
5.chapter: Pathogenesis & Irido-Zonulo-Hyaloido-Vitrectomy (IZHV) Management of Aqueous Misdirection
5.quote: Aqueous misdirection presents with uniform central and peripheral AC shallowing and elevated/normal IOP despite a patent PI. Miotics are strictly contraindicated; initial atropine, aqueous suppressants, and hyperosmotics are followed by Nd:YAG hyaloidotomy or definitive surgical irido-zonulo-hyaloido-vitrectomy (IZHV) establishing a unicameral eye.

mcqs.q: On postoperative day 3 after trabeculectomy in a short hyperopic eye with PACG, the IOP is 36 mmHg, the bleb is flat, the peripheral iridotomy is patent, and BOTH the central and peripheral anterior chamber are uniformly flat. Which drug is strictly contraindicated and what is the definitive surgical cure if medical/laser therapy fails?
options: Atropine is contraindicated; surgical peripheral iridectomy is the definitive cure
Oral acetazolamide is contraindicated; Palmberg compression sutures are the definitive cure
Topical prednisolone is contraindicated; posterior sclerotomy drainage is the definitive cure
Pilocarpine is contraindicated; irido-zonulo-hyaloido-vitrectomy (IZHV) is the definitive cure
mcqs.explanation: This presentation is classic aqueous misdirection (malignant glaucoma). Pilocarpine worsens anterior rotation of the ciliary body and is strictly contraindicated; definitive surgical cure requires creating a permanent unicameral eye via irido-zonulo-hyaloido-vitrectomy (IZHV).

mcqs.q: A 76-year-old aphakic, high-myopic patient develops acute excruciating pain, IOP of 42 mmHg, flat anterior chamber, and dark-brown dome-shaped choroidal mounds with high-reflectivity clots on B-scan 48 hours after Baerveldt GDD surgery. After starting systemic steroids, cycloplegics, and IOP-lowering therapy, what is the optimal timing for secondary surgical drainage if central retinal apposition ('kissing') persists?
options: Immediate drainage within 2 hours of hemorrhage onset to prevent fibrosis
Delayed drainage at 7–14 days once serial B-scan ultrasonography confirms clot liquefaction
Observation for 6 months because hemorrhagic choroidals always resolve spontaneously without retinal damage
Immediate Nd:YAG laser disruption of the choroidal mound through the pupil
mcqs.explanation: Immediate drainage of an acute clotted suprachoroidal hemorrhage is ineffective and risks catastrophic re-bleeding; optimal timing is typically 7–14 days after onset once serial B-scan confirms clot liquefaction, particularly when kissing choroidals, flat AC, or intractable IOP/pain persists.

mcqs.q: A patient with an avascular, thin-walled MMC trabeculectomy bleb created 4 years ago presents with a mucopurulent bleb, 2 mm hypopyon, dense vitritis, and hand-motion vision. Which pathogen is most commonly implicated and what is the recommended definitive intervention?
options: Cutibacterium acnes; topical moxifloxacin monotherapy without intravitreal injections
Staphylococcus epidermidis; observation with subconjunctival gentamicin only
Streptococcus species; prompt pars plana vitrectomy with vitreous biopsy plus intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime
Pseudomonas aeruginosa; immediate bleb needling with 5-fluorouracil
mcqs.explanation: Late-onset bleb-related endophthalmitis (BRE) is predominantly caused by virulent Streptococcus species (carrying a dismal prognosis), and early pars plana vitrectomy combined with intravitreal vancomycin (1 mg) and ceftazidime (2.25 mg) is favored even when visual acuity is better than light perception.
